title: Separate Odd and Even
directAnswer: Create two lists; append each element to the even or odd list based on `x % 2 == 0`. Order is preserved by appending as you scan.

remember.takeaway: Appending while you scan preserves relative order automatically.
remember.formula: even=[x for even]; odd=[x for odd]   (stable by append)
whenToUse: Splitting into groups while preserving order

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums`, return a pair of lists: all even numbers and all odd numbers, each in their original relative order.
understanding: One pass; route each element into the even or odd output list.

approaches.name: Route into two lists
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Route each element into an `even` or `odd` output list based on its parity. Appending in scan order makes the partition **stable** — each group keeps its original relative order — for free.

**Why appending preserves order.** You read left to right and append to the back of the matching list, so within each bucket the elements appear in the same sequence they had in the input. No sorting or extra bookkeeping is needed.

**Two output lists vs in place.** Producing two separate lists is O(n) extra space but simplest. An in-place stable partition is harder; an *unstable* in-place partition (two-pointer swap) is O(1) space but reorders within groups — mention the trade-off.

**Parity robustness.** Test `% 2 == 0` so negative evens are bucketed correctly.

code.python:
def separate(nums: list[int]) -> list[list[int]]:
    even = [x for x in nums if x % 2 == 0]
    odd = [x for x in nums if x % 2 != 0]
    return [even, odd]

hints: Two output buckets — what decides which one an element goes to?
Appending as you scan preserves each group's order automatically.
approaches.complexityReasoning: one parity test and one append per element; two lists hold n elements total, so O(n) space.

dryRun.intro: Append to the matching bucket in scan order.

pitfalls: Inserting at the front and reversing a group's order.

commonMistakes: Reversing one group by inserting at the front.
